content: Pressure ulcers are areas of localized damage to the skin and underlying tissue, caused by factors such as pressure, shear, friction, or a combination of these forces. Electromagnetic therapy (EMT) involves the use of electrodes to generate an electromagnetic field across a wound, and it has been proposed as a potential method to enhance the healing of chronic wounds, including pressure ulcers. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of EMT on the healing of pressure ulcers. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL, with the most recent search performed on June 10, 2015. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared EMT with either sham EMT or standard treatment. Two review authors independently screened the search results to identify relevant RCTs. Full reports of potentially eligible studies were obtained, and data extraction was performed. Any disagreements between the authors were resolved through discussion. In previous versions of the review, attempts were made to contact study authors to retrieve missing data. No new trials were identified in this update. The original review included two RCTs involving a total of 60 participants. Both studies were assessed as having an unclear risk of bias. These trials compared EMT with sham EMT, and one of the studies also included a third group that received only standard therapy. Neither trial demonstrated a statistically significant difference in the rate of complete healing between participants treated with EMT and those in the control groups. One of the trials reported a statistically significant difference in the percentage reduction of wound surface area in favor of EMT. However, this finding should be interpreted with caution due to the small sample size of the study, which increases the likelihood that the result may be due to chance. Furthermore, the outcome of percentage reduction in wound area is considered less clinically meaningful than the outcome of complete wound healing. In conclusion, the evidence does not strongly support the use of EMT for the treatment of pressure ulcers. However, the possibility of either a beneficial or harmful effect cannot be definitively ruled out, as the review included only two small trials with methodological limitations. Further research is recommended to better understand the potential role of EMT in managing pressure ulcers.
